query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: If AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock is processed using a cold spray additive manufacturing (CSAM) technique instead of conventional high-thermal-load (e.g., laser powder bed fusion) regimes, then the resulting miniature components will exhibit significantly reduced residual thermal stresses and improved mechanical properties (e.g., higher ductility and lower brittleness), due to the absence of melting/solidification and associated thermal gradients.
generation.material_initial_state: Gas-atomized AlCrFeNiSi alloy powder, particle size suitable for additive manufacturing (e.g., 10–50 μm), stored under inert atmosphere.
generation.intervention: Replace high-thermal-load additive manufacturing (e.g., laser or electron beam melting) with cold spray additive manufacturing, where powder particles are accelerated at high velocity and consolidated via solid-state impact at substrate temperatures well below melting.
generation.conditions: Processing at substrate temperatures below 0.5 Tm (where Tm is the melting temperature of AlCrFeNiSi), using a cold spray system with carrier gas (e.g., N2 or He) at 300–800°C, for miniature components (<10 mm characteristic dimension), under inert or controlled atmosphere to prevent oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of nanocrystalline or as-atomized microstructure, absence of solidification microsegregation, and minimization of thermal gradients and associated residual stresses.
generation.mechanism: Cold spray avoids melting and rapid solidification, thus eliminating the primary source of residual thermal stresses and microstructural inhomogeneities. The high-velocity impact induces severe plastic deformation and bonding without significant heating, preserving the feedstock's microstructure and preventing phase segregation or grain coarsening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi components, cold-sprayed parts will show (1) lower residual stress (by at least 50%), (2) higher ductility (by at least 20%), (3) comparable or improved yield strength, and (4) reduced processing complexity (no need for preheating, post-processing heat treatment, or support structures for thermal management).
generation.baseline: Miniature AlCrFeNiSi components fabricated by laser powder bed fusion under standard parameters (e.g., laser power 200–400 W, scan speed 500–1500 mm/s, build plate at 100–200°C), exhibiting typical residual stresses, microsegregation, and as-built mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: Applicable to miniature components (<10 mm), AlCrFeNiSi alloy feedstock, and cold spray systems capable of achieving particle velocities >500 m/s. Not applicable to geometries requiring internal channels <100 μm or overhangs unsupported by cold spray.
generation.uncertainty: The degree of mechanical property improvement depends on the cold spray process parameters and the ability to achieve full density and interparticle bonding. Some loss of strength may occur if bonding is incomplete. The hypothesis assumes that cold spray can achieve near-full density and adequate bonding for this alloy system.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components: one by cold spray additive manufacturing under optimized conditions, and one by conventional laser powder bed fusion. Characterize both sets for residual stress (e.g., X-ray diffraction), mechanical properties (tensile/compression tests), and microstructure (SEM/TEM).
measurements: Ductility (elongation to failure in tensile test)
Microstructure (grain size, phase distribution by SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If cold-sprayed components do not show at least 20% lower residual stress and 10% higher ductility compared to conventionally processed counterparts, or if their density is <95% of theoretical, the hypothesis is falsified.
